Shanghai

Where tradition meets tomorrow

Shanghai is a city of layers — Art Deco heritage buildings hiding Michelin-worthy dumpling shops, rooftop cocktail bars above 1930s slaughterhouses, and water towns that feel frozen in the Ming dynasty. Beyond the Bund clichés lies a city that rewards the curious.

Shanghai Natural History Museum (上海自然博物馆)

Housed in a stunning building shaped like a nautilus shell, designed by an international architecture firm. World-class exhibits on dinosaurs, evolution, and earth sciences. The atrium alone is breathtaking — a vast sunlit space with hanging whale skeletons and towering dinosaur fossils. TripAdvisor's top-rated Shanghai museum.

510 Beijing West Road, Jing'an District Line 13 Natural History Museum Station

Propaganda Poster Art Centre (宣传画艺术中心)

A truly unique and quirky private museum hidden on the basement floor of a residential building. Houses one of the world's largest collections of original Chinese propaganda posters from the 1950s-1980s. Fascinating window into China's political and social history. Run by a passionate collector. Very off-the-beaten-path — you'd never find it without knowing about it.

726 Yanan Road West (Bldg 2B, Basement) Line 10/11 Jiaotong University Station

Shanghai Museum (People's Square) (上海博物馆)

One of China's four great museums, housing over 1.2 million pieces of ancient Chinese art. World-renowned for its bronze, ceramics, calligraphy, and jade collections. The building itself is inspired by an ancient bronze vessel. Free entry with online reservation. Plan 2-3 hours minimum.

201 Renmin Avenue, Huangpu District Line 1/2/8 People's Square Station
Open in AMap

Shanghai Postal Museum (上海邮政博物馆)

China's first museum dedicated to postal history, located in the magnificent 1924 neo-classical Shanghai General Post Office building overlooking Suzhou River. Reopened in December 2024 after extensive renovation with enhanced exhibits tracing China's communication evolution.

Tiantong Road, Hongkou District Line 3/4/10 Tiantong Road
Open in AMap
🏛️
Free

Shanghai Meteorological Museum (上海气象博物馆)

Housed in the 1872 Xujiahui Observatory — one of China's earliest weather stations and one of only two founding stations of the global meteorological network. The museum features an extraordinarily rare 1850 barometer (one of only five in the world), vintage seismographs, and century-old weather instruments. Known as Shanghai's hardest-to-book museum, it requires advance reservations but rewards visitors with a fascinating journey through 150 years of atmospheric science in a gorgeous heritage building.

Jing'an Temple (静安寺)

One of Shanghai's most famous ancient Buddhist temples, dating back 1,800 years. Stunning golden rooftops visible from the street, surrounded by modern skyscrapers. The contrast between ancient temple and futuristic city is uniquely Shanghai. Three halls with exquisite Buddha statues and a peaceful central courtyard.

Duoyunxuan Art Center (朵云轩艺术中心)

A century-old stationery brand (founded 1900) reinvented as a 30,000 sqm cultural complex. The highlight is its woodblock watermark printing workshop — one of only two institutions in China still practicing this intangible cultural heritage craft, capable of producing near-perfect reproductions of classical Chinese paintings. The center also houses master studios, a Southern intangible heritage exhibition, and an art cinema.

Open in AMap
🏯
¥10

Longhua Temple (龙华寺)

Shanghai's oldest and largest Buddhist temple, founded in 242 AD during the Three Kingdoms period. The seven-story pagoda is an iconic landmark. Far fewer tourists than Jing'an — a genuinely peaceful experience. The vegetarian noodles at the temple canteen are legendary.

2853 Longhua Road, Xuhui District Line 11/12 Longhua

79 Creative Park (79意库)

A former 1950s factory complex in Minhang reborn as one of Shanghai's most photogenic creative parks. The industrial-chic design blends raw brick walls, steel beams, and weathered textures with minimalist white galleries and pop-up art installations. Part of the Greater Zero Bay innovation corridor, it attracts designers and photographers drawn to its Instagram-worthy alleys and vintage-meets-modern aesthetic.

🎨

Bridge 8 Creative Park (8号桥创意园区)

Shanghai's pioneering creative-industry conversion — the former Shanghai Auto Brake Factory (1970s), transformed in 2003 into a loft-style hub for designers and artists. Its name comes from the colorful block-arch bridges linking the old factory buildings. The compact campus in the former French Concession houses design studios, boutique shops, and cafes, with original industrial bones — exposed brick, steel trusses, and sawtooth roofs — beautifully preserved.

Open in AMap
🎨
Free

Yunjian Granary Cultural and Creative Park (云间粮仓文创园)

A sprawling 9-hectare complex of 59 former grain warehouses and factories (1950s-1990s) at the confluence of the Renmin and Tongbo canals in Songjiang. Eight colossal 24-meter-tall silos stand as the park's landmark. The renovated space hosts an art gallery, a beer museum, graffiti murals, and riverside cafes. The Songjiang South Gate Barn has been reborn as a castle-like fashion and art landmark blending Soviet-era industrial architecture with contemporary art.

Guilin Park (桂林公园)

A serene classical Chinese garden originally built in the 1930s as the private estate of Shanghai figure Huang Jinrong. The park is planted with over 1,000 osmanthus trees that fill the air with fragrance in autumn. Its pavilions, rockeries, lotus ponds, and zigzag bridges offer a tranquil escape from the surrounding urban bustle — a hidden gem that most tourists walk right past.

Bugao Li Shikumen Alley (步高里)

One of Shanghai's best-preserved shikumen longtang (stone-gate alleyway) complexes, built in 1930 in the French Concession era. Its distinctive arched stone entrance bears the carved characters '步高里' and a French inscription, reflecting the city's Franco-Chinese heritage. The narrow lanes retain their original red-brick facades, carved wooden doors, and the intimate communal atmosphere of old Shanghai — a living architectural museum hidden in plain sight.

A massive 20-venue urban entertainment complex in central Shanghai combining nightlife, immersive experiences, dining, and live music all under one roof. Secret Roof

A hidden rooftop cocktail bar perched atop Zhang Garden in Shanghai's Jing'an District. Yuyintang Livehouse (育音堂)

One of Shanghai's oldest and most legendary live music venues, operating since 2004. The newest incarnation at 851 Kaixuan Road backs onto Tianshan Park. This flagship venue is the beating heart of Shanghai's underground and indie music scene, hosting local bands, underground acts, and occasional international touring artists. Fuxing Island (复兴岛) - Shanghai's Only Inland River Island

Shanghai's hidden island gem — the only inland island on the Huangpu River, a treasure trove of industrial heritage and colonial history. Fuxing Island features a fascinating mix of abandoned warehouses, old shipyard facilities, art installations, and quiet riverside paths. Once a bustling industrial zone, the island has been gradually reimagined as a cultural space with galleries and creative studios. Easily accessible by public transport, it offers a peaceful retreat with skyline views across the Huangpu. A perfect spot for photographers, urban explorers, and anyone interested in Shanghai's industrial past. Recommended by Shanghai's official tourism portal as a hidden weekend getaway.

Chongming Island Xisha Wetland (崇明岛西沙湿地)

Shanghai's secret coastal escape — a vast wetland paradise on Chongming Island, the world's largest alluvial island at the mouth of the Yangtze River. Xisha Wetland offers a rare glimpse of pristine coastal ecology within Shanghai's borders. The wetland features winding boardwalks through reed marshes, bird-watching towers, tidal flats teeming with crabs and mudskippers, and a famous 'pearl lake' perfect for sunset viewing. In spring, the area comes alive with blooming flowers and migratory birds. Designated as one of Shanghai's official scenic springtime routes. A perfect day trip for nature lovers wanting to escape the concrete jungle — accessible by ferry or the Yangtze River Bridge tunnel.

Beijing

Emperors, alleyways, and everything after

Beijing isn't just the Forbidden City and Great Wall. It's underground techno clubs in former bomb shelters, 400-year-old courtyard villages you can stay in, the world's best Peking duck in holes-in-the-wall, and temples older than most countries.

Beijing Customs Museum (北京海关博物馆)

A hidden gem museum in Beijing that receives almost no tourists, offering visitors an immersive private experience. The Beijing Customs Museum showcases the fascinating history of China's customs and trade through centuries — from ancient Silk Road commerce to modern port operations. Exhibits include historical artifacts, antique customs equipment, smuggling case displays, and interactive presentations. The museum is quiet, uncrowded, and completely free to visit, making it a perfect off-the-beaten-path cultural experience. Recommended by travelers in 2026 as one of Beijing's best lesser-known museums.

Beijing Stone Carving Art Museum (北京石刻艺术博物馆)

Located inside the Ming Dynasty Zhihua Temple (五塔寺) complex near the National Library, this underrated museum houses over 500 ancient stone carvings spanning 2,000 years of Chinese history. The centerpiece is the Five Pagoda Temple itself — a stunning Indian-style Vajra Throne Pagoda from the Ming era adorned with carved Buddhas and Tibetan motifs. A magnificent 500-year-old ginkgo tree turns the grounds golden each November, creating one of Beijing's most breathtaking autumn scenes with virtually no crowds.

Beijing Planetarium (北京天文馆)

China's first and largest planetarium, recently upgraded with a state-of-the-art 8K dome theater that delivers breathtaking immersive journeys through the cosmos. Beyond the dome shows, the facility features interactive astronomy exhibits, meteorite specimens, and a solar telescope for daytime observation. The combination of cutting-edge projection technology and accessible science education makes it a must-visit for space enthusiasts of all ages.

No. 93 Courtyard Museum (93号院博物馆)

A tiny 160-sqm traditional siheyuan in an authentic old hutong near Dashilar, serving as a hands-on intangible cultural heritage base. Visitors can watch and try making Mao Hou (hairy monkey figurines from cicada shells and magnolia buds), clay sculptures, Peking opera face masks, kites, and paper cuttings — all under the guidance of resident craftsmen. Completely free to enter and rarely crowded.

A workshop and storefront on the 600-year-old Yangmeizhu Byway run by 5th-generation Tu'erye (Rabbit God) inheritor Zhang Zhongqiang. The tiny shop overflows with colorful clay rabbit deities — a traditional Beijing folk art dating back 400+ years — in every pose and outfit imaginable. Zhang offers hands-on painting sessions where you can customize your own rabbit god figurine.

Langyuan Vintage (郎园Vintage)

A low-density creative district carved from the former Beijing Wandong Medical Equipment Factory, right in the heart of the CBD near Guomao. Twelve old factory buildings totaling 30,000 sqm were renovated starting in 2009 into a cultural strip combining offices for creative agencies, an international boutique street, and a 6,000 sqm fashion show venue. The contrast of rusted industrial facades against the gleaming CBD skyline makes it a favorite for urban explorers.

Fahai Temple (法海寺)

A hidden 1439 Ming Dynasty temple nestled in the foothills of Shijingshan District, famous for housing some of the finest surviving Buddhist frescoes in all of China — comparable to the Dunhuang Caves in artistic importance. The interior murals, painted by master craftsmen using mineral pigments and gold leaf, remain vivid after nearly 600 years. Access to the fresco hall is strictly limited to 25 visitors at a time with mandatory guided tours, preserving both the art and the intimate, reverent atmosphere of this remarkable treasure.

Zhihua Temple (智化寺)

A hidden Ming Dynasty temple (1444) in a hutong alley that most tourists walk right past. Famous for its daily performances of Beijing Temple Music (京音乐), a 600-year-old living tradition using Ming Dynasty instruments. Intimate courtyard with original Ming wooden architecture.

77 Cultural and Creative Park (77文创园)

A hidden creative gem in Dongcheng District, transformed from a 1950s offset printing factory into a vibrant cultural and creative industrial park. Nestled behind quaint gray brick walls on Art Gallery Back Street (画廊后街), the park retains many industrial relics from the original factory including massive printing presses and exposed steel beams. Now houses art exhibitions, indie galleries, design studios, boutique cafes, and co-working spaces. The contrast between raw industrial architecture and contemporary art creates a visually stunning atmosphere perfect for photography and creative inspiration. One of Beijing's most authentic factory-to-art transformations.

751D·PARK Beijing Fashion Design Plaza (751D·PARK北京时尚设计广场)

A 220,000 sqm former gas-production plant from 1952, sister to the adjacent 798. After gas production ceased in 2003, the colossal industrial infrastructure — towering gas holders, pipelines, and furnace halls — was repurposed as Beijing's fashion and design epicenter. The raw post-industrial aesthetic with massive steel structures and exposed concrete draws photographers and design lovers, while Beijing Design Week events keep the creative energy high.

Beijing Makerspace (北京创客空间)

One of China's earliest and most influential maker communities, this Zhongguancun space has incubated numerous hardware startups since its founding. Equipped with CNC machines, soldering stations, 3D printers, and a comprehensive materials library, it bridges the gap between hobbyist tinkerers and professional product development. Their weekly 'Maker Night' events are legendary in Beijing's DIY scene, offering a welcoming entry point for anyone curious about making things.

China's Silicon Coast

Shenzhen gets dismissed as a factory city. Wrong. It has the country's best contemporary art scene, pristine beaches the locals don't want tourists to know about, Hakka villages older than Hong Kong, and a creative energy that makes Brooklyn look sleepy.

Shenzhen Museum (深圳博物馆)

The main museum of Shenzhen covering the city's transformation from fishing village to megacity in just 40 years. Fascinating exhibits on urban planning, reform-era history, and local Lingnan culture. Interactive displays make it engaging even for non-history buffs. Free entry.

Citizen Center, Futian District Line 4 Civic Center Station
Open in AMap
🏛️
Free

China Ancient Iron Museum (中国历代熨斗博物馆)

A Guinness World Record-holding private museum hidden inside a converted Hakka watchtower in Longgang District, displaying an astonishing collection of over 1,600 antique irons spanning 2,000 years of Chinese history. From bronze hand-pressers used in the Han Dynasty to ornate Qing Dynasty charcoal-heated models and early electric irons, the collection traces the evolution of this everyday object in surprising detail. The museum is free but requires arranging access through the village service center due to irregular opening hours.

Guanlan Original Printmaking Base (观澜版画原创产业基地)

A beautifully preserved Hakka village in Bao'an District transformed into China's premier printmaking art village, where international artists live, work, and exhibit in converted ancestral homes. The cobblestone lanes wind between traditional Hakka architecture and modern print studios, while the on-site museum houses works by masters from over 40 countries. The combination of rural heritage and contemporary art, plus the free entry and peaceful atmosphere, makes it one of Shenzhen's most rewarding cultural escapes.

Xiangmi Park (香蜜公园)

A strikingly designed urban park opened in 2017 that blends ecology with art and community spaces in the heart of Futian District. Elevated boardwalks wind through tree canopies, a 4,000-plant rose garden bursts with color year-round, and the park houses a public library and an elegantly designed marriage registration hall. Water features, native plantings, and a resource-recycling station make it a model of sustainable urban landscape design.

Futian Mangrove Ecological Park (福田红树林生态公园)

Shenzhen's only state-level inland wetland park, a 38-hectare ecological treasure in the heart of Futian District. The park is a coastal wetland sanctuary where humans and nature coexist in harmony — home to diverse bird species, mangrove forests, and tidal flats. Open daily from 6AM to 11PM, it features scenic walking trails, bird-watching platforms, and an ecological restoration area. Despite being in the center of one of China's most developed cities, the park feels like a pristine natural escape. An essential visit for nature lovers, photographers, and anyone seeking green tranquility amid Shenzhen's urban buzz.

Shenzhen produced 2.75 million civilian UAVs in the first half of 2025 alone — this is where the drone revolution is most visible.

Bantian Handcraft Culture Street (坂田手造文化街)

A quietly atmospheric Hui-style architecture street in Longgang District built as a haven for traditional Chinese craftsmanship. Despite being less known than Shenzhen's trendy art districts, it hosts active workshops for woodblock printing, tie-dyeing, traditional jewelry-making, and Hanfu photography. The campus with its sweeping eaves and stone-paved paths offers a rare slow-lifestyle counterpoint to Shenzhen's high-speed energy.

Open in AMap

Nantou Ancient City (南头古城)

A 1,700-year-old walled city in Nanshan District transformed from a neglected urban village into one of Shenzhen's most compelling creative districts. The 2017 UABB triggered an artistic intervention that draped formerly crumbling village walls with vivid graffiti and murals. Today, narrow historic lanes weave between Qing-dynasty ruins, indie bookshops, design studios, craft coffee roasters, and street art — a living palimpsest of Shenzhen's entire history from fishing village to tech metropolis.

Xiyuo Town (西柚小镇)

Shenzhen's first graffiti-themed commercial street, hidden in the Guangming District near Xiachun Park. The former village neighborhood was revitalized with 59 large-scale creative murals covering building facades, turning every corner into a burst of color. The block includes maker co-working spaces, hip cafes, and street-food stalls, creating a laid-back, artsy atmosphere that feels worlds away from Shenzhen's tech-campus stereotype.

Shenzhen's most spectacular coastal hiking trail, stretching along the dramatic eastern coastline of Dapeng Peninsula. This 8-10km trail combines rugged mountain paths with breathtaking ocean views, passing hidden beaches, sea caves, and the iconic Chuanbi Rock natural sea arch. The trail connects Xichong Beach (Shenzhen's longest and most pristine beach) to Dongchong village, winding through coastal cliffs with panoramic views of the South China Sea. Rated as one of China's most beautiful coastal walks. The natural sea arch at Chuanbi Rock is a landmark highlight that reopened in April 2026 after restoration. A must-do for hikers and coastal scenery enthusiasts visiting Shenzhen.

Dapeng Peninsula, eastern Shenzhen Bus from Dapeng Station (Line 8)

Jiaochangwei Village (较场尾) - Shenzhen's Little Hawaii

A charming seaside village on Shenzhen's Dapeng Peninsula, known as the 'Little Hawaii of Shenzhen.' Jiaochangwei features rows of colorful guesthouses and homestays along the beach, creating a Mediterranean village feel. The village sits right on a golden sand beach with calm waters perfect for swimming and water sports. Once a quiet fishing settlement, it has transformed into a trendy coastal getaway while retaining its original village character. Visitors can enjoy fresh seafood, beachside cafes, surfing lessons, and stunning sunsets. Located near Dapeng Fortress, it pairs perfectly with a historical visit. A favorite weekend escape for Shenzhen locals seeking coastal vibes without leaving the city.

Dapeng Peninsula, eastern Shenzhen (near Dapeng Fortress) Bus from Dapeng Station (Line 8)

Nan'ao Island (南澳岛) - Shantou's Pristine Island Getaway

A stunning island off the coast of Shantou in eastern Guangdong, accessible as a day trip from Shenzhen via high-speed rail. Nan'ao Island is Shantou's crown jewel — a subtropical paradise with crystal-clear waters, golden sand beaches, and dramatic sea cliffs. The island features Qing'ao Bay (the first Blue Flag beach in China), ancient fishing villages, a 17th-century coastal fort, wind farms on mountain ridges, and fresh seafood feasts at local restaurants. The island's mountain roads offer spectacular panoramic views of the Pacific Ocean. Connected to the mainland by the spectacular Nan'ao Bridge (one of China's longest sea-crossing bridges), it's a perfect coastal road trip destination from Shenzhen (about 3 hours by car).

Nan'ao Island, Shantou (3hrs from Shenzhen by HSR + car) Shantou Station (HSR from Shenzhen North)

Gulangyu Island, Xiamen (鼓浪屿) - UNESCO World Heritage Car-Free Island

A UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of Fujian's most enchanting destinations, located a 5-minute ferry ride from downtown Xiamen. This pedestrian-only island is packed with colonial-era mansions, lush gardens, winding narrow lanes, and sandy beaches. Once a foreign concession with 13 different country consulates, the architecture blends East meets West in stunning fashion. The island is famous for its piano museum, organ museum, ocean views from Sunlight Rock, and the Shuzhuang Garden. No cars or bicycles are allowed — only electric buggies and walking, creating a uniquely peaceful atmosphere. A perfect stop along the Shanghai-Shenzhen high-speed rail route (2.5hrs from Shenzhen by HSR). One of China's most romantic and photogenic coastal spots.

Xiamen, Fujian (2.5hrs from Shenzhen by HSR) Xiamen Station (HSR) + ferry from Dongdu Pier

Quanzhou Maritime Silk Road Heritage (泉州海丝遗迹)

Quanzhou, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2021, was the Eastern starting point of the Maritime Silk Road and one of the busiest ports in the world during the Song and Yuan dynasties. Located in Fujian Province along the high-speed rail route between Shanghai and Shenzhen (accessible from Xiamen in 30 minutes by train), Quanzhou's ancient city hides 22 World Heritage spots among its historic lanes. Highlights include the towering Kaiyuan Temple with its twin pagodas, the Tianhou Temple dedicated to the sea goddess Mazu, ancient stone bridges, Islamic tombs, and the atmospheric West Street (西街) food district. The city offers an authentic glimpse into China's golden age of maritime trade, with the ancient port area now beautifully restored as a cultural district.

Guangzhou Maritime Museum (广州海事博物馆)

Guangdong's only dedicated maritime museum, opened in 2021, located next to the historic Nanhai God Temple — a key site on the ancient Maritime Silk Road. The museum's striking modern architecture houses exhibits spanning 2,000 years of Guangzhou's maritime trade history, including ancient shipwreck artifacts, porcelain exports, navigational instruments, and interactive displays about the Maritime Silk Road. Its location in Huangpu District connects it directly to the city's port heritage, making it a perfect companion visit to the nearby Huangpu Ancient Port.

Huangpu Ancient Port (黄埔古港)

Guangzhou's historic river port that served as the main entry point for foreign merchants during the Qing Dynasty's Canton System (1757-1842). This beautifully restored heritage area on the Pearl River's eastern bank was where all international trade ships docked before Canton became fully open. Today, the ancient port features a museum with excavated ship relics, traditional Lingnan architecture, old guild halls, and atmospheric lanes lined with street food stalls serving Cantonese snacks. The area comes alive in the evening with local diners enjoying riverside meals. A fascinating blend of maritime history, heritage preservation, and authentic Guangzhou food culture. Recognized as one of Guangzhou's most important historical waterfront sites.

Huangpu District, Guangzhou Line 4/8 Wanshengwei

Renwei Temple (仁威祖庙)

A 1,000-year-old Taoist temple quietly sitting by Liwan Lake in the heart of traditional Xiguan, featuring some of the finest Lingnan-style wood carvings, ceramic ridge decorations, and clay sculptures in all of Guangzhou. Despite its historical significance and exquisite craftsmanship, the temple receives virtually zero tourist crowds — most visitors are local elderly residents who come to burn incense and chat. The temple's intimate scale, beautifully detailed corridors, and peaceful lakefront setting make it one of Guangzhou's most rewarding hidden cultural treasures.

Haizhu Wetland Park (海珠国家湿地公园)

China's only national wetland park situated on the central axis of a megacity, covering a massive 1,100 hectares in Guangzhou's Haizhu District. This ecological masterpiece is Guangzhou's 'green heart' — a vast expanse of wetlands, lakes, camphor forests, and flower fields right in the middle of the city. Famous for its spectacular spring bougainvillea and autumn seas of golden reeds. The park features a 2.65km loop trail around Haizhu Lake, bird-watching towers, orchid gardens, and ancient camphor tree groves. Over 10 years of ecological restoration have transformed it from degraded land into a biodiversity hotspot with over 180 bird species. A must-visit for anyone seeking nature within the city.

A small, exquisitely designed classical Lingnan-style garden specializing in orchids, tucked away near Yuexiu Park. Far less visited than its famous neighbor, it offers a meditative retreat in the heart of the city.

Features interactive exhibits on robotics, AI, digital effects, and technology history including a Digital Revolution exhibition with bilingual Mandarin/English content. Houses multiple science cinemas, robot shows, and a digital manufacturing lab.

Guangzhou's beloved board game specialty store and community hub, known for organizing the annual Guangzhou BGM Board Game Exhibition — one of South China's biggest tabletop gaming events. TIT Creative Park (T.I.T创意园)

A landmark industrial-reuse project occupying the former Guangzhou Textile Machinery Factory, built in 1952. After creative renovation, the site retains its red-brick chimneys, rusty industrial pipes, and sawtooth-roof workshops — now accented with colorful graffiti walls, greenery, and floor-to-ceiling glass. Tech companies like KuGou Music sit alongside design studios and coffee shops, making it Guangzhou's template for factory-to-creative-park transformation.

B.I.G Haizhu Bay Art Park (B.I.G海珠湾艺术园区)

A riverside creative park carved from the Daganwei Wharf Warehouse Complex built in the 1950s on the southern bank of the Pearl River's Haizhu channel. The renovated warehouses feature massive two-story graffiti murals visible from across the river. By day it's a workspace for design agencies; by night, locals gather at waterfront bars and pop-up events. The blend of raw industrial heritage, large-scale street art, and Pearl River sunset views makes it one of Guangzhou's most atmospheric creative hangouts.

The leafy back lanes of Dongshan are lined with 1920s-1930s villas built by overseas Chinese. Red-brick garden houses with arched windows, iron gates, and banyan-draped walls. Several have been converted into indie cafés and galleries but the residential atmosphere is intact.

Shamian Island Lanes (沙面岛巷弄)

A tree-shaded island in the Pearl River with over 150 colonial-era buildings from the French and British concession era. The narrow lanes are canopied by massive banyan trees. Walking here feels like being in a European country town. Historic architecture includes churches, consulates, and banks.

Enning Road Historic Lanes (恩宁路历史文化街区)

The last intact stretch of traditional Xiguan-style alleyways in Guangzhou. Features Lingnan-style manors (西关大屋), qilou arcade buildings, and the birthplace of Cantonese opera master Xue Juexian. The area is being gently restored — not over-commercialized yet.

Huangdong Ancient Temple (黄埔古村洪德古庙)

A hidden Ming Dynasty temple in Guangzhou's ancient Huangpu Village, predating the city's modern history. The village itself is a time capsule of traditional Lingnan architecture with ancestral halls, banyan-lined lanes, and oyster-shell walls. The temple holds seasonal traditional ceremonies.

Huangpu Flight Academy

Guangzhou's premier drone pilot training center, located on Changzhou Island at the mouth of the Pearl River. Offers professional UAV (unmanned aerial vehicle) pilot certification courses for multi-rotor and VTOL fixed-wing drones. Has attracted researchers from Tsinghua University and is well-known in the drone industry for its comprehensive training programs.

Guangzhou Science City

A massive government-supported technology park and innovation district in Huangpu, envisioned as China's future smart manufacturing center and international tech innovation hub. Home to numerous high-tech companies, research institutes, and incubators spanning electronic information, biotech, pharmaceutical, and environmental technology industries.

Open in AMap

Guangzhou Nansha Low-Altitude Economy & Robot Experience Hub

Guangzhou's emerging 'Silicon Valley' for unmanned systems in Nansha District, combining robot retail, robotic coffee, drone delivery trials, and autonomous bus rides in one destination. Visitors can ride eVTOL (electric vertical takeoff and landing) aircraft simulators, watch drone food deliveries, interact with service robots making coffee and playing chess, and ride autonomous shuttle buses. Guangzhou is scaling the AI and robotics innovations born in Shenzhen into consumer-ready experiences. Part of Guangdong's plan to build a world-class low-altitude economy cluster.

Guangzhou Nansha International Robot Industrial Park

Nansha's emerging robotics and low-altitude economy hub, part of Guangzhou's Greater Bay Area tech corridor. Features robot manufacturing facilities, drone testing zones, and intelligent logistics demonstrations. Nansha is positioning itself as Guangzhou's answer to Shenzhen's robotics ecosystem.

Nansha Jiaomen River Autonomous Boat Cruise (南沙蕉门河无人船观光)

Guangzhou's first unmanned autonomous sightseeing boat cruise on the Jiaomen River. Part of the Greater Bay Area Full-Space Unmanned System Demonstration Point. The autonomous boat uses ultrasonic radar and vision cameras for obstacle avoidance. Features air-conditioned cabin with sofas and karaoke.

XPENG AEROHT eVTOL Manufacturing Base (小鹏汇天飞行汽车智造基地)

XPENG AEROHT, XPeng's flying car subsidiary and Asia's largest low-altitude eVTOL company, operates its manufacturing and experience base in Huangpu District. Produces the 'Traveler' series flying cars and demonstrated the X3 at the 2024 Zhuhai Airshow. China's first manned eVTOL airworthiness certification received in 2024.
